To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cultured human, rat and mice hepatocytes can be induced by carcinogens to develop ultrastructural changes commonly observed when liver cells are exposed to carcinogens.

1) the nucleolus is a sensitive target for carcinogen-induced alterations in the ultrastructure of hepatocytes in vitro and 2) the sensitivity of human, rat and mice hepatocytes to carcinogen-induced nucleolar segregation is similar to that observed in vivo.

the nucleolar segregation induced in cultured hepatocytes by carcinogens correlates with their carcinogenicity in vivo and that human, rat and mice hepatocytes in primary cultures can be used to determine the relative sensitivity of human liver to carcinogenesis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing in vitro systems to evaluate the carcinogenic potential of chemicals.

the use of cultured human hepatocytes to study the mechanisms of action of carcinogens, to develop a model system for the study of human hepatocarcinogenesis and to develop an assay system for the evaluation of the carcinogenicity of chemicals.
the development of an in vitro system to evaluate the potential toxicity of environmental chemicals and pharmaceuticals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
human hepatocytes are more sensitive than rat hepatocytes and rat hepatocytes more sensitive than mouse hepatocytes to the toxic effects of actinomycin, AFB1 and DMN.

the nucleolar segregation observed in human, rat and/or mouse hepatocytes exposed to these carcinogens in vitro was a dose-dependent effect and that the relative sensitivity of the three species to the carcinogens was similar to their relative sensitivity to the carcinogens in vivo.
nucleolar segregation is a reliable indicator of the carcinogenic activity of chemicals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
human hepatocytes were the least sensitive, mouse hepatocytes the most sensitive, and rat hepatocytes were intermediate in sensitivity.
human hepatocyte cultures are more resistant than rodent hepatocyte cultures to the toxic effects of AFB1 and DMN.
the nucleolar segregation is an early, non-specific response to DNA damaging agents.
The main takeaway from our work is that
human hepatocytes are more sensitive to carcinogens than rodent hepatocytes.

hepatocytes can be used for the study of the effects of chemicals and drugs on liver cells and that the effects of these compounds on hepatocytes in vitro are similar to the effects observed on hepatocytes in vivo.

hepatocyte cultures may be a good system to determine the relative sensitivity of human liver to carcinogens and that the sensitivity of the liver of humans, rats and mice to the toxicological effects of carcinogens is similar.
